# Survivalist — art sheets

Generated by the `/art-sheets` bench (`src/views/ArtSheets.vue`, dev only).
**Do not hand-edit the generated files** — re-run the bench instead. This
README and `painted/` are the only things in here a human writes to.

Survivalist ships with zero gameplay bitmaps of its own: the cast is hand-inked
vector art baked to frame strips at runtime, and the road, the gates, the crates
and every effect are Canvas 2D. These sheets are that cast baked out through
the renderer's OWN painters, so it can be handed to an image model, repainted in
a **dark-fantasy** hand, and sliced back in as drop-in bitmaps that register
against the drawing each one replaces.

```
  procedural renderer  ──bench──▶  walk-*.png / still-*.png  +  PROMPTS-*.md  +  sheet-index.json
                                              │  image model (Gemini / Nano-Banana, ChatGPT, Midjourney)
                                              ▼
                                   art-sheets/painted/*.png
                                              │  pnpm slice-sheets
                                              ▼
                                   public/images/<kind>/<id>.webp
                                              │  ?art=on  (spriteFor probes, behind a flag)
                                              ▼
                                   the game, drawing paint instead of vectors
```

---

## Two shapes of sheet

**Walk cycles** — `walk-<design>.png` for the thirteen monsters and
`walk-hero-<outfit>.png` for the three survivors. A 4 × 2 grid of 320 px
panels (1280 × 640, 2:1), each panel the bake's own frame box scaled up, each
panel one moment of ONE locomotion cycle. What comes back is cut on the same
grid into one horizontal strip, and the game plays that strip from the same
clock that drives the procedural bake — the swap is seamless mid-stride.

**Stills** — `still-<kind>-<id>.png`, one object per image, for every prop,
gate frame, round, effect, backdrop band, the HUD's marks (the crown, the
result banner, the shop chest, the two skill icons) and the logo. A still is a
one-panel walk to the slicer, which is what gives it the same fit step: the
return is measured against the reference and normalised onto it, so a crate
painted with a polite margin still fills its box in play.

The **survivors' sheets** carry a panel-by-panel script in their prompt: a
run seen from behind is eight distinct leg positions or it is nothing, and the
first returns held one pose for two panels because the reference of the time
did too. The reference now draws a back-view run (the swing boot folding up
with its sole showing, a flight moment between strides) and the prompt names
what each panel is.

The key sheets (`key-walks.png`, `key-stills.png`) are the human contact sheet:
every reference at thumbnail size with its name and target. Nothing is ever
written inside a panel — text inside a frame is text a model will repaint.

## The box is the contract

Every still is drawn by the game's own painter (`useSurvivalArt.ts`) into
**exactly the rectangle the game blits the painting back into**, and every walk
panel through the bake's own frame painter. The bench carries no sizes of its
own. That is the whole reason the round trip is mechanical: the return is fitted
onto the reference's measured box (`fit` in `sheet-index.json`, measured on
solid pixels so a glow is light rather than extent), so a painting that came
back too big, too small or off-centre lands where the drawing was.

Where the game paints something LIVE over a bitmap, the reference leaves it out
and the prompt says so:

| painting | what stays live on top |
| --- | --- |
| crates | the coloured rim, the badge, the HP number |
| barricade | hazard chevrons, damage bar, HP number |
| powder keg | damage cracks, the lit strobe |
| pillar | the warning glow, the hot overlay, the beacon, the topple |
| gate frames | the curtain, the chevrons, the number plate, the charge meter |
| rolling boulder | the scrolling bands that sell the roll |
| bomb | the spark walking down the fuse |
| shield dome | the ground ring, the crest, the countdown arc |
| boss guard | the crest over it |
| rocket | the blast when it lands |
| result banner | the title, printed across the middle band |
| skill icons | the cooldown ring and the seconds count |

A few boxes are deliberately BIGGER than the drawing they hold, because the
painting carries detail the drawing does not: the roller's sphere sits at
1/1.3 of its file so the spikes have somewhere to go, and a ring, the dome and
the guard sit at 1/1.12 so their glow does not run off the edge. The runtime
blits those files larger by the same factor (`ROLLER_ART_PAD`, `FX_PAD` in
`useSurvivalArt.ts`), so the shape inside lands exactly on the radius the game
measures against — and the prompt states the fractions, because those stills
are not fitted onto the reference.

The **result banner** is nine-sliced by CSS rather than drawn whole: the
outer 17% of the width at each end is kept at true size and the middle is
stretched to the title, so the file's 21:9 shape is only the end pieces'
shape, and all of a painting's detail has to live in those ends (`BANNER` in
`uiArt.ts` is the one number the drawing, the prompt and the stylesheet share).
The **skill icons and the chest** are referenced as the buttons' own glyphs —
white silhouettes — and the prompt describes the treatment.

Two things the game does to the painting that the painter must not do first:
the **rounds** are authored at rest, pointing RIGHT (the tracer UP), and turned
to their heading by the renderer; the **ridge bands** are black silhouettes
tinted per stage by the renderer. The **smoke puff** is greyscale and tinted per
emitter.

## The prompts

`PROMPTS-WALKS.md` and `PROMPTS-STILLS.md` carry one ready-to-paste block per
sheet, generated from the manifest (`src/game/artSheet.ts`) so every sheet
briefs the same style and the same background contract. The order of the
blocks is load-bearing — what comes back, what it must not be, what it is, the
style lock, the layout, the magenta rule, a count-and-check list, the exact
output pixels — because image models weight what they read first and last.

**Ask for magenta, never transparency.** A transparent background comes back
as the grey-and-white checkerboard painted in as pixels. A flat `#FF00FF` ground
is something a model can actually draw, and the slicer keys it out (a channel
test: green under 70 with red and blue over 190 — nothing in this palette is
near it; the multiplier gate's prompt says *deep violet, never magenta* for
exactly that reason).

**Set your image tool's aspect ratio to match the sheet.** A square return of
a 2:1 walk sheet cannot be cut. The slicer forgives a uniform squash of up to
15 % on a walk and resizes a still to its target, but not a re-composed grid.

**When a return is bad, fix the prompt, not the file.** A hand-fixed bitmap is
a fix that will not survive the next re-roll.

## Getting art back into the game

**1 · Drop the repainted images in `art-sheets/painted/`.** Any filename that
still contains the sheet's name works — `walk-grumpling.png`,
`walk-grumpling-v3.png`, `still-prop-coin.png`. The slicer matches the longest
name it recognises. PNG, ideally; JPEG smears magenta into every edge.

**2 · Slice them:**

```
pnpm slice-sheets                     # everything in art-sheets/painted/, 256 px per frame
pnpm slice-sheets --dry               # print the plan, write nothing
pnpm slice-sheets art-sheets/painted/walk-grumpling.png
pnpm slice-sheets --sheet coin x.png  # force the target when the name is odd
pnpm slice-sheets --size 512          # force a different frame height for one run
```

What the slicer does for you, and what it refuses to guess about:

* keys out the magenta, de-fringes the rim, unmixes soft edges, and floods a
  white/cream/checkerboard ground away when the key found nothing;
* measures the grid it actually got back and refuses to shred a walk sheet
  whose panels are not where the index says (`--frames <n>` accepts a
  different count as one cycle; `--take-rows 2` cuts only the top two rows of
  a return that doubled the grid, which a low, wide creature invites);
* re-composes a gate frame: finds both posts from the doorway outward, anchors
  each by its inner face on the reference's band (squeezing one that came back
  wider), stretches the lintel between them, throws away anything painted
  below the lintel in the doorway, and stands the frame on the ground line —
  because image models paint heavy gate posts whatever the prompt says;
* fits every return onto the reference's box with ONE correction for the whole
  strip, anchored by the feet for a creature and the falling rock and by the
  middle for everything else, and prints what it corrected;
* caps every frame at **256 px tall by default** — the size the payload and
  the eye have agreed on in every project so far — lowered to the manifest's
  `maxEdge` where that is smaller (a coin is 20 px in play, a crown 12),
  raised to the biggest resized copy a sheet ships, and never upsampled from
  the return; a still the manifest marks `exact` (the logo — the PWA manifest
  reads that file at 512) is written at its own size whatever is asked;
  `--size <px>` forces a different height for one run;
* writes the logo as PNG at the two sizes the PWA manifest reads;
* warns on a JPEG, a non-magenta ground, a dropped frame, feet that drift
  between frames, a creature redrawn at different scales, and a subject that
  came back as a solid card.

**3 · Look at it in motion**, in `/playground` (dev only): every drawable
through the game's own painters, with a dashed box around what each is
allowed to occupy and one button that flips the art layer live. A painted part
is only ever wrong *relative* to the drawing it stands in for.

**4 · Measure what the eye misses:**

```
python tools/measure-art.py strips public/images/monsters       # eaten frames
python tools/measure-art.py pairs public/images/props --ref-prefix still-prop-
python tools/measure-art.py pairs public/images/rounds --ref-prefix still-round-
```

**5 · Turn it on:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| `?art=on` | Use the bitmaps. **Remembered**, so the param can be dropped afterwards. |
| `?art=off` | Back to the procedural art. Also remembered. |
| `__art.on()` / `__art.off()` | Same, live from the console — no reload. |
| `__art.refresh()` | Re-read the files from disk after re-slicing, without a reload. |
| `__art.status()` | `{ enabled, source, probes }` — `source` is `url`, `stored` or `build`. |

**6 · To ship it enabled**, set `VITE_ENABLE_ART_OVERRIDES=true` in the build's
env. It is off by default and **must stay off in every `.env.<platform>` until
the art is in** — with no override art shipping, every probe misses, and
CrazyGames' QA console reports each miss as `Missing resource detected`, one
line per drawable, which reads as a broken build. A miss is never an error for
the game itself; the drawing keeps drawing.

With the flag on, the splash holds for a stage's worth of art (`artPreload.ts`
derives it from the stage the player resumes to), the next stage's newcomers
and this stage's threats follow one at a time, and the whole set arrives on an
idle slot — so a first-time player on a phone pays for stage 1, not for a
boss they meet on stage 9.

## Regenerating

```
pnpm dev                                   # port 2050
open http://localhost:2050/#/art-sheets    # click "Export all sheets"
pnpm art:export                            # or headless, in a private Chrome
```

Everything animated is frozen at a fixed phase, so a re-export is
byte-identical unless the art actually changed — a diff here means something in
the renderer moved.
